metric_rationale: This is signed top-cue endorsement: +1 when the subject follows the uniquely highest-validity cue and -1 when they override it. It uses all 96 trials, including mirrored A/B versions, so response-side tendencies cancel and each subject's estimate is relatively precise. Take The Best predicts a positive score at every evidence level because the first cue always discriminates. Tallying predicts zero contribution on the two tally-tie conditions and negative contributions on the ten conditions where the accumulating lower cues defeat the top-cue winner. Thus the theories place the metric on opposite sides of zero, producing a larger and more stable separation than a slope based on only a subset of evidence levels.

This is a signed high-validity-cue alignment score: +1 when a choice follows the first discriminating cue in validity order and -1 when it opposes that cue. Because every designed pair has an equal tally, Tallying predicts independent guessing and hence an expected score of 0. Take The Best predicts the first discriminating cue's option, producing an expected score of (1-epsilon)*tanh(beta/2), which is positive for every allowed parameter combination. Pooling all 96 trials gives a low-noise within-subject estimate, while the option-swapped mirrors ensure that generic A/B response bias cannot create a positive score. The metric tests a behavioral covariance between choices and cue rank rather than merely overall choice proportions.

This is a preregistered configuration-sensitivity covariance after orienting every stimulus toward its 3-cue tally winner. The centered weight is the majority-choice probability predicted by a fixed midpoint instantiation of Accessibility-Balanced Evidence Integration. Thus configurations where the majority coalition occupies strong late cues receive positive weights, while configurations where its three cues are outweighed by two late cues receive negative weights. Under Tallying, every oriented trial has the identical 3-versus-2 margin and hence the same expected majority-choice rate; centering the weights makes its expected metric exactly zero for every beta and epsilon. The advocated theory predicts that observed majority choice covaries strongly with these weights. All 96 responses contribute to the scalar, mirror trials are automatically placed in the same canonical orientation, and the balanced repeated schedule keeps the per-subject estimate comparatively stable. The weights are fixed independently of responses rather than fitted to the observed data.

This is an accessibility-weighted rate of choosing the option supported by the later of the two discriminating experts. It recodes the mirrored A/B trials into a common direction, thereby cancelling response-side preference, and pools all repetitions so it remains stable at the individual-subject level. Tallying gives every trial an exact 0.5 probability because each option wins one cue. Accessibility-Balanced Integration instead predicts increasingly frequent selection of the later-supported option as its supporting cue moves farther down the display. The exponential contrast weight is a matched-filter approximation based on the midpoint of the competing theory's recency-gradient range: it downweights the weak, noisy nearest-position contrast and emphasizes trials on which the competing theory predicts its largest departure from chance.

This is the proportion of choices favoring the option with greater exponentially recency-weighted cue support. In every designed conflict, that option is the adjacent late-cue coalition rather than the coalition supplying the final discriminating cue. Accessibility-Balanced Evidence Integration therefore predicts values above 0.5, whereas Switch-Closure Coalition Integration predicts values below 0.5 because its balanced-coalition closure gate favors the opposite option. The six exact A/B mirrors make the measure insensitive to a stable A-versus-B response bias. Averaging all 96 binary observations gives a stable per-subject estimate, while the fixed midpoint recency gradient avoids estimating noisy subject-level parameters.

The metric measures the theories' clearest opposing qualitative prediction while remaining response-side invariant. For every trial it identifies the option supported by Experts 1–3, pools all 96 mirrored and repeated trials within each subject, and asks whether that option wins a majority of the subject's choices. Switch-Closure Coalition Integration predicts majority support for this early coherent three-cue coalition; Accessibility-Balanced Evidence Integration predicts majority opposition because its later two-cue coalition receives greater accessibility weight. Averaging a subject-level majority indicator sharply reduces trial-level choice noise, while the exact A/B mirrors prevent a generic preference for response A or B from producing the effect.

This metric is the weighted difference in endorsement of the three-cue coalition between entry-compact configurations ([adjacent cue, then gap]) and their exit-compact counterparts ([gap, then adjacent cue]). It recodes choices relative to the three-cue coalition, so the exact A/B mirrors cancel response-side bias. It also contrasts configurations within the same 3-versus-2 coalition sizes, cue validities, onset, and number of adjacent links, removing stable subject differences in overall preference for larger coalitions. Reliability-Compressed Parsing Mixtures predicts a positive contrast for every integration style, with a larger effect at wider gaps; the bounded gap weight emphasizes those more diagnostic trials while retaining all 96 observations. Switch-Closure Coalition Integration assigns matched entry- and exit-compact configurations the same structural gate because their onset and adjacency coherence are identical, predicting a contrast near zero.

This is the within-subject early-versus-late change in endorsement of the three-cue coalition, coded independently of whether that coalition is displayed as A or B. Switch-Closure Coalition Integration predicts a positive contrast because its amplified near-balance gate favors the three-cue coalition when it begins before the two-cue coalition and disfavors it when it begins afterward. Reliability-Compressed Parsing Mixtures predicts the same three-cue endorsement rate in both groups: coalition sizes and internal gap patterns are fixed, and its relevant parsing descriptor is translation-invariant. Averaging 48 observations on each side uses every trial, while the within-subject difference cancels stable integration-style effects, general preference for three versus two cues, and response-side tendencies; the mirrored pairs further balance A/B assignment.
